newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe seems to have new lease on life.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe seems to have new lease on life.

text.p: Don't whisper it too loud, but French Prime Minister Alain Juppe is enjoying the timid beginnings of a political comeback.

Viewed as a liability by many in his centre-right coalition and subject to constant sniping from conservative rivals last year, his opinion poll ratings have risen from rock bottom and President Jacques Chirac has given him a new lease on life.

Political analysts say Juppe has benefited from Chirac's decision to take a more active domestic role and by his determination to press ahead with reforms after a period of hesitation and back-pedaling in late 1996.

"Both in the coalition and in the public, it has begun to sink in that the president is standing by Juppe. That has given him a chance of staging a comeback in popularity before the 1998 parliamentary elections," a cabinet minister told Reuters.
But political analysts say his chances of a durable recovery depend on whether he can engineer a revival in economic growth and a decline in record 12.7 percent unemployment this year.

The latest BVA institute poll shows Juppe's approval rating has gained six points in a month, rising from an all-time low of 20 percent to 26 percent, after the publication of a slim book in which he projected a more human, less technocratic image.
Even among the 68 percent who still have a negative opinion of him, many voters credit him with the virtues of courage, honesty, determination and in some cases competence.

Juppe's emotional book, "Entre Nous" (Between ourselves), launched in a media blitz that featured glossy pictures of Juppe with his baby daughter Clara and a more public role for his wife Isabelle, has become a bestseller.

As recently as early December, it seemed nothing could go right for Juppe. The government caved in to a truck drivers' blockade, conceding retirement at 55. The privatisation of defence and electronics giant Thomson came unstuck and Juppe was forced to stall or retreat on other unpopular measures.
The turning point was probably a December 12 television interview in which Chirac, breaking a long silence, ruled out a rumoured cabinet reshuffle and voiced full support for Juppe.
He insisted the prime minister was courageously implementing reforms necessary to modernise France.

The impact was not immediate, but Chirac has since made two more broadcasts and a series of policy speeches, launching an ambitious shake-up of the justice system this week and stressing that other reforms -- some deferred last year -- will go ahead.

"The president has launched more than just a justice reform. He has relaunched his term politically...with a new sharing of roles with his prime minister," commentator Paul Guilbert said in an editorial in the conservative daily Le Figaro.
"The president fixes the aims of national ambition and gives a sense of direction. The government, answerable to him, then sets out 'action plans,"' he wrote.

Since the start of the year, the government has introduced controversial legislation to create private pension funds in the National Assembly and a bill to reform the heavily indebted SNCF state railways in the Senate.
The prime minister has said he is determined to go ahead with the sale of a 20 percent stake in state telecommunications company France Telecom to the public this spring.

In another break with the past, Juppe's office said on Tuesday he would no longer set an annual ceiling for pay rises in state-owned companies, leaving each firm to negotiate according to its own financial position.

The strength of the franc suggests that financial markets have confidence in Juppe's ability to qualify France for a single European currency by keeping this year's public sector deficit to around three percent of gross domestic product.

However, the labour situation remains tense, as this week's occupation of ailing property lender Credit Foncier shows, and Juppe could still be vulnerable to a fresh wave of unrest in France's volatile workforce.
Questioned by the left-wing daily Liberation, opinion pollsters differed on Juppe's prospects of a sustained return to public favour, noting his ratings remained low.
"The very fact that he is settling in for the longer term will lead him to regain a bit of popularity," said Philippe Mechet of the Sofres polling institute.

But Roman Pache of the BVA institute, while saying voters credited Juppe with "mitigating circumstances", said: "As long as the premier doesn't achieve results in the fight against unemployment, his standing will remain fragile."
